intro: You can stop most interview scheduling back and forth by offering specific times in one message, then letting the candidate pick from a short list. Scheduling polls and booking pages help when a panel is involved. This page shows what the thread costs, why it keeps happening, and fixes you can use this week without buying anything.
tldr: 67% of recruiters in a 2019 Yello survey say one interview takes 30 minutes to 2 hours to schedule.
Panels make threads grow fast. Research on group scheduling finds the odds of success drop significantly past five people.
Name a window in your first email, write the time zone next to it, and set a limit on rounds.
Free options include a window list, a Gmail template, a scheduling poll on a work account, and a Google booking page on a personal account.
Lazur explains settings, points at controls, dictates and drafts replies. It does not send invites or click buttons for you.

blocks.text: A single interview thread looks small. One email asks for times. Another offers one. A third says that time no longer works, and the loop starts again. Multiply that by every candidate, every panelist and every reschedule, and the hours add up fast.
What interview scheduling back and forth costs you

The clearest number comes from Yello's 2019 survey of 200 recruiting professionals. In that survey, 67% said scheduling one interview takes between 30 minutes and 2 hours. Another 17% said two to five hours. These are recruiter estimates, not time logs, so treat them as a rough guide. Time one of your own threads to check the numbers against your week.

The cost is not only your time. Yello also reports that 60% of recruiters say they sometimes or often lose candidates before an interview is booked. Cronofy's 2024 candidate report covered about 12,000 candidates in seven countries. It found 42% of candidates say they leave a process when scheduling takes too long, down from 49% a year earlier. Cronofy sells scheduling software, so read that as what candidates say, not measured drop-off.

blocks.text: Hiring managers feel the drag too. Robert Half's April 2025 survey of more than 2,200 US hiring managers lists scheduling and conducting interviews among the parts of hiring that take more time. 43% said so. The same survey found 93% say hiring takes longer than it did two years ago. SHRM's benchmark puts average cost per hire at nearly $4,700. That figure covers all roles, so it is not a scheduling bill. It does show what a slow hire costs.
Why interview scheduling turns into back and forth

Most threads are not caused by rude candidates or slow managers. They come from a few structural problems. Nobody can see everyone's free time at once. So you ask, get a partial answer, and ask again. The fixes below work because they remove one of those problems.

Panels make it worse. A 2024 Case Western Reserve study on group scheduling, reported by Phys.org, found the chance of a successful meeting drops significantly when more than five people are involved. The number of candidate times you must poll also grows exponentially with participants. The original paper was not available when this page was written, so this comes from press coverage.
The calendar problem on Mac

Apple Calendar on Mac has no booking page. Apple's help says Check Availability shows invitees' free times only for calendar services that track availability, such as CalDAV. Whether you can propose a new time also depends on the service. Check your calendar account type before you assume a shared view will work. Apple's help does not say whether replies are sent automatically.
Edge cases that break the simple fixes

items: Personal Gmail accounts cannot use Microsoft's Scheduling Poll, so send a window list or a Google appointment schedule instead.
Shared mailboxes cannot be the organizer for a Scheduling Poll, so the organizer must be a person.
A panel member who will not vote can stall a poll. Keep a plain window list in the same email as the poll link.
Phone screens and video screens may need different lengths. Create one event type for each, or send a window list.
Agency recruiters who work for several clients need separate calendars, so one client's availability does not leak into another client's invite.

blocks.title: Check candidate data rules
blocks.text: Candidate names, CVs and contact details are personal data. Before you paste them into an AI tool, check your employer's policy. Lazur sends audio and the screenshot to AI providers only while you hold the shortcut and ask. They are not stored, and content is not used to train AI models.
Worked example: a panel, a hiring manager and a candidate abroad

Say a candidate lives in Lisbon. You work in Chicago, and the hiring manager is in London. The panel needs about an hour together. The old way starts with a message asking when the candidate is free. The candidate offers a couple of mornings. The hiring manager cannot make either. The thread grows, and a week passes.

The new way starts with the panel. If your account supports a poll, send it to the interviewers first and pick the slot that works for them. Then write one email to the candidate. It names the time, the time zone, the length and who will join. It also includes a fallback window in case the candidate cannot make it. The candidate now has one decision to make.
Mistakes people make when they try to fix it

items: Sending a poll to people whose account does not support it, then waiting for replies that never come.
Writing a time without the time zone. Candidates often read it in their own zone and arrive at the wrong hour.
Offering only the slots that are already tight on your calendar, then rejecting the first pick.
Sending a booking link without opening it on a phone first.
Changing the plan in the middle of the thread without telling the candidate what changed.

blocks.text: A quieter mistake is the template that never gets updated. If your window email still lists last quarter's days, you will send bad times. Review your saved reply each time your panel changes. Read the times aloud before you send, because your eye skips over old dates.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. It lives in the notch, and you hold a key to talk to it. For this problem it does three things well. It explains a setting while you look at it, it points at the control you need, and it drafts or dictates the reply. It does not send invites for you, and it does not click buttons.

Dictation saves time on the messages you send all week. Hold fn and speak the email. Lazur types clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Then read it before you send. In Gmail in Chrome, ⌘Return sends the message. In Apple Mail, ⌘⇧D sends. You own every message, so check each one.
A one week plan to cut the thread

The plan below fits one week. Each step takes about as long as one scheduling email. You do not need a new tool to start. The first two days cost nothing except a little setup time, and the rest only needs your calendar and your inbox.
What to do next

Start with your next interview. Write the window email, put the time zone in every line and set a round limit. Keep a count of emails for that thread. Compare it with your last one. If the thread is still long, add a booking page or a poll for panels, but test it on one interview first.

If you want help with the steps, Lazur has a free trial with no credit card. The [pricing page](/pricing) lists the plans. For the Gmail side, the [Gmail guide for recruiters](/for/recruiters/gmail) covers templates and follow-ups.

faq.question: Does Lazur send interview invites for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur explains settings, points at controls, guides you one click at a time, dictates and drafts text. It does not click buttons or operate other apps. You send the invite and the reply yourself.

faq.question: Can I use a scheduling poll with a Gmail address?
faq.answer: Not with Microsoft's Scheduling Poll. Microsoft says it does not support Gmail, Yahoo, or other POP or IMAP accounts, or Outlook.com consumer accounts. Check your account type first, then pick a window list or a Google appointment schedule.

faq.question: Do Google appointment schedules work on a Mac?
faq.answer: Google requires a supported web browser and a personal or Workspace account. Google does not name Mac in its help page, but a browser on your Mac fits its requirement. Create the schedule in the browser, not the Calendar app on a phone.

faq.question: What is the cheapest way to stop scheduling back and forth?
faq.answer: Start with a window email that names the time zone. It costs nothing. Calendly's free plan includes one event type. Its Standard plan is $10 per seat per month billed yearly, per Calendly's pricing page.

faq.question: Why does Apple Calendar have no booking page?
faq.answer: Apple's Calendar help for Mac covers invitations and Check Availability, but it does not document a booking page. Check Availability depends on the calendar service. For a booking page, use a Google appointment schedule or a dedicated scheduling tool.

faq.question: How many emails should a thread take before I call?
faq.answer: No source gives a single right number. Pick a rule that fits your team, write it down, and keep to it. Calling after the first back-and-forth is a practical starting point for many recruiters.

faq.question: Is it safe to use AI tools with candidate details?
faq.answer: Follow your employer's rules first. Lazur sends audio and a screenshot to AI providers only while you hold the shortcut and ask. They are not stored, and content is not used to train AI models. Do not share candidate data your policy forbids.

costs.title: Recruiter hours
costs.text: Yello's 2019 survey of 200 recruiting professionals found 67% say scheduling one interview takes 30 minutes to 2 hours. Another 17% say two to five hours. Those are self-reported estimates, so time one of your own threads to compare.

costs.title: Candidates who walk away
costs.text: Yello reports that 60% of recruiters say they sometimes or often lose candidates before an interview is booked. Cronofy's 2024 survey found 42% of candidates say they leave when scheduling takes too long. Cronofy sells scheduling software, so that figure reflects what candidates say, not measured drop-off.

costs.title: Hiring managers waiting
costs.text: Robert Half's April 2025 survey of more than 2,200 US hiring managers lists scheduling and conducting interviews among the parts of hiring that take more time. 43% said so. Each week a role stays open is time your team spends without the hire.

costs.title: Money per hire
costs.text: SHRM's benchmark puts average cost per hire at nearly $4,700. That covers all roles, not scheduling alone. A slow thread delays the whole hire, so it adds to a cost that is already high.

causes.title: Open questions invite partial answers
causes.text: When you ask when someone is free, they list what they remember, not what they have checked. That is a partial answer, and each partial answer starts one more round. A window you name in advance cuts the loop, because the candidate only has to say yes or pick one.

causes.title: Nobody can see everyone's free time
causes.text: Calendars often cannot show invitees' free and busy time. Apple's Calendar help says Check Availability works only for calendar services that track availability, such as CalDAV. So you guess, ask, and guess again.

causes.title: Time zones hide the overlap
causes.text: A slot that fits your day can land in the middle of the night for a candidate abroad. People convert times in their heads, and they often get it wrong. Writing the zone in each message removes that step.

causes.title: Panels multiply every question
causes.text: A 2024 Case Western Reserve study, reported by Phys.org, says the chance of a successful meeting drops significantly above five people. The number of times you must poll grows exponentially with participants. A panel with several interviewers and a hiring manager sits in that range.

causes.title: Reschedules restart the thread
causes.text: One cancellation can undo a confirmed slot. Each reschedule sends the thread back to the start, with new questions and new partial answers. A reschedule line in your template keeps the loop shorter when plans change.

causes.title: No one owns the thread
causes.text: When a recruiter, a coordinator and a hiring manager all reply, nobody picks the final time. Name one owner in the first email, and say who will confirm the slot. That single line stops three people from answering the same question.

fixes.title: Offer a short window, not an open question
fixes.text: Pick a short list of windows from your calendar and put them in the first email. Write the time zone next to each window. Ask the candidate to reply with one. A pick ends the loop faster than an open question does. This works in any email app, and it costs nothing.

fixes.title: Use a scheduling poll for panels
fixes.text: If you have a Microsoft work or school account, Scheduling Poll lets people vote on up to 15 time options. Voters can change their votes until the organizer picks a final time or the poll expires. Microsoft says it replaces the FindTime add-in. It does not work with Gmail, Yahoo, or other POP or IMAP accounts, and shared mailboxes cannot be organizers. Microsoft's poll article does not list Outlook for Mac, so check the steps in your version first.

fixes.title: Use a Google appointment schedule
fixes.text: A personal or Workspace Google account can publish a booking page for interviews. Google says you need a supported web browser, and you cannot create the schedule in the Calendar app on iPhone or iPad. The default minimum lead time is 4 hours, and you can cap bookings per day. Some features need an eligible Workspace or Google One plan.

fixes.title: Try a free booking page first
fixes.text: Calendly's free plan is always free and includes one event type. That fits one interview format, such as a standard screen call. Its Standard plan is $10 per seat per month billed yearly. Its Teams plan is $16 per seat per month billed yearly and adds round-robin scheduling. Check calendly.com/pricing before you choose, because plans change.

fixes.title: Call after the first back-and-forth
fixes.text: Set a rule that you call after the first back-and-forth, not after several. A short phone or video call can settle a time in one exchange. Write the rule in your notes, and mention it in your first email so the candidate knows a call may come.

fixes.title: Save your best scheduling reply
fixes.text: Write the reply once with the window format, the time zone line and the round rule. Save it as a Gmail template and reuse it. Read the times aloud before each send, because a copied time is the most common error.

plan.label: Monday
plan.title: Count your last threads
plan.text: Open Gmail and search for your last few interview threads. Count the emails in each one and write the counts down. That gives you a baseline to beat next week.

plan.label: Tuesday
plan.title: Write one window email
plan.text: Draft a reply that offers a short list of windows and asks for a time zone. Save it as a Gmail template. Keep it short, so a candidate can answer in one line.

plan.label: Wednesday
plan.title: Put the time zone in every invite
plan.text: Add the time zone to each invite title and to each email that offers a time. In the Calendar app, press ⌘N to start a new event, then check the time zone before you send.

plan.label: Thursday
plan.title: Test a booking page on a phone
plan.text: If your account supports a Google appointment schedule, or if Calendly's free plan fits, set up one interview type. Open the link on your phone and book a test slot. Cancel the test booking afterward.

plan.label: Friday
plan.title: Set your round limit
plan.text: Decide how many emails a thread gets before you call. Write that rule in your notes. Tell your hiring manager, so they expect the call when it comes.

plan.label: Next week
plan.title: Compare the thread counts
plan.text: Count the emails on your next few threads, using the same method as Monday. Keep the steps that shortened the thread and drop the ones that did not help.
